ECE 6390 / Antennas and arrays

Solid angle and power

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows why a polar-angle step and an azimuth step need an area weight before they can represent radiated power.

To find total radiated power, collect the power crossing every patch on a sphere around the antenna. A ring at polar angle θ has radius R sinθ, so an azimuth step dφ covers arc length R sinθ dφ. The perpendicular polar step has length R dθ.

The patch area is therefore dA = R² sinθ dθ dφ. Dividing by R² gives solid angle dΩ in steradians. Radiation intensity U in W/sr multiplied by dΩ gives watts in that patch. Near the pole, equal angular rectangles cover less area.

A complete sphere subtends 4π sr. An ideal forward-only element radiates over 2π sr, yet directivity still uses 4π times intensity divided by total radiated power. Omitting sinθ overweights polar samples and produces the wrong normalization.

Example

A uniform 2 W/sr source has total power 8π W over a full sphere. A patch with θ from 55° to 65° and φ width 30° has solid angle (π/6)(cos55° − cos65°), about 0.079 sr, so it carries about 0.158 W.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. Compare small equal-angle patches centered at θ = 30° and θ = 90°. Which has more solid angle, and by what factor?

    For sufficiently small patches, all factors except sinθ cancel.

    The equatorial patch at 90° has twice the solid angle because sin90°/sin30° = 2.

    2. Why is integrating only the main lobe insufficient for absolute directivity?

    The denominator represents all radiated power.

    Sidelobes and grating lobes also carry power. Omitting them underestimates total power and overestimates directivity. A restricted integration is justified only after the excluded contribution is bounded.
